note.explanation: A deforming force can change an object's size or shape. Elastic materials return to their original size and shape when the force is removed. For a spring, the spring constant tells us how much force is needed for each unit of extension.
examples: A spring stretches when a load is hung from it and returns to its original length when the load is removed.
A tennis ball and the racket strings deform when the ball is hit; they regain their original shapes after the ball bounces away.
note.checkAnswer: An elastic object returns to its original size and shape after the deforming force is removed.
note.simple: Push, pull or squeeze something and its shape or size may change. If it returns to its original shape when you stop, it is elastic.
note.checkQuestion: What happens to an elastic object when its deforming force is removed?
note.title: How forces deform solids
steps: A force that changes an object's size or shape is called a deforming force.
A spring can be stretched (extended) or squeezed (compressed).
An object is elastic if it restores its original size and shape after the deforming force is removed.
The property that allows it to do this is called elasticity.
For a spring, spring constant is calculated using k = F/x, where F is force and x is extension.
note.answer: Elasticity is the property by which a material restores its original size and shape after the deforming force is removed.

options: A force that changes an object's size or shape
A force that changes an object's mass
A force that changes an object's temperature only
A force that changes its colour
mcqs.stem: What is meant by a deforming force?
rationales: Correct: a deforming force changes an object's size or shape.
Incorrect: changing mass is not the definition of a deforming force.
Incorrect: a deforming force is defined by a change in size or shape, not temperature alone.
Incorrect: changing colour is not the defining effect of a deforming force.

options: It restores its original size and shape
It keeps the changed shape permanently
mcqs.stem: What happens to an elastic object after its deforming force is removed, provided it has not exceeded its elastic limit?
rationales: Correct: an elastic object restores its original size and shape.
Incorrect: keeping the changed shape permanently describes a permanent deformation.
Incorrect: removal of a deforming force does not make an object lose mass.
Incorrect: elasticity does not cause an object to start moving by itself.

mcqs.stem: What is the property of a material that allows it to restore its original shape after a deforming force is removed?
rationales: Correct: this property is called elasticity.
Incorrect: density is mass per unit volume, not the ability to restore shape.
Incorrect: pressure is force per unit area, not the ability to restore shape.
Incorrect: inertia is resistance to a change in motion.

options: A steel spring, within its elastic limit
mcqs.stem: Which is the best example of an elastic object when used within its elastic limit?
rationales: Incorrect: clay dough does not normally return to its original shape after deformation.
Correct: a spring restores its original shape when the force is removed, provided its elastic limit is not exceeded.
Incorrect: plasticine is an inelastic material in the example given in your textbook.
Incorrect: wax that stays bent has not restored its original shape.

mcqs.stem: Which equation gives the spring constant k in terms of force F and extension x?
rationales: Correct: spring constant is force divided by extension, k = F/x.
Incorrect: this is the reciprocal of the required relationship.
Incorrect: multiplying force by extension does not give the spring constant.
Incorrect: adding force and extension does not give the spring constant.

mcqs.stem: What is the SI unit of spring constant?
rationales: Correct: k = F/x, so its unit is newton per metre, N m⁻¹.
Incorrect: N m is a unit of work or energy, not spring constant.
Incorrect: kg m⁻³ is a unit of density.
Incorrect: Pa is a unit of pressure.

options: It does not regain its original shape or size
Its spring constant must become zero
mcqs.stem: What happens when a material is deformed beyond its elastic limit?
rationales: Correct: the change becomes permanent and the object does not regain its original shape or size.
Incorrect: passing the elastic limit does not remove the object's weight.
Incorrect: the definition concerns permanent deformation, not necessarily a zero spring constant.
Incorrect: exceeding the elastic limit does not turn a solid into a liquid.

options: The deformation changes the size or shape of the object
The object is necessarily in motion
The object must be a liquid
mcqs.stem: When a tennis ball hits racket strings, why are the ball and strings said to be deformed?
rationales: Correct: the hit changes their shapes temporarily.
Incorrect: deformation does not mean that an object has no mass.
Incorrect: motion alone is not what is meant by deformation.
Incorrect: the ball and strings are solids, not liquids.

written.text: What is Hooke's law? Does an object remain elastic beyond elastic limit? Give reason.
written.finalAnswer: Within the limit of proportionality, the extension of a spring is directly proportional to the applied force. An object does not remain elastic beyond its elastic limit because the change becomes permanent and it does not regain its original shape or size after the deforming force is removed.

written.text:
A spring having spring constant k hangs vertically from a fixed point. A load of weight L, when hung from the spring, causes an extension x, the elastic limit of the spring is not exceeded. Some identical springs, each with spring constant k, are arranged as shown below:

For each arrangement, complete the table by determining:
(i) the total extension in terms of x.
(ii) the spring constant in terms of k.

| Arrangement | Total Extension x | Spring constant (k) of the arrangement |
|---|---|---|
| [FIGURE: Two springs arranged vertically in series, hanging from a fixed support, with a load labelled L at the bottom.] | | |
| [FIGURE: Two springs arranged in parallel between a fixed support and a horizontal bar, with a load labelled L hanging from the bar.] | | |
written.finalAnswer: Series: total extension = 2x; spring constant = k/2. Parallel: total extension = x/2; spring constant = 2k.

rubric.why: In series, each identical spring carries the full load and extends by x.
rubric.description: Find the total extension for the series arrangement.
rubric.how: Add the two extensions x + x to obtain 2x.

rubric.why: The equivalent spring constant must produce extension 2x under load L.
rubric.description: Find the spring constant for the series arrangement.
rubric.how: Use k arrangement = L/(2x) and L = kx, giving k/2.

rubric.why: In parallel, the load is shared equally, so each spring extends by x/2 and the bar moves that distance.
rubric.description: Find the total extension for the parallel arrangement.
rubric.how: State that the parallel arrangement extends by x/2.

rubric.why: Two parallel springs have the combined effect of both spring constants.
rubric.description: Find the spring constant for the parallel arrangement.
rubric.how: Add the constants k + k to obtain 2k.

modelAnswer: For one spring, L = kx.
Series: each spring carries load L, so each extends by x.
Total extension in series = x + x = 2x.
Spring constant in series = L/(2x) = kx/(2x) = k/2.
Parallel: the identical springs share the load equally, so each carries L/2.
Extension of each spring = (L/2)/k = x/2; hence total extension = x/2.
Spring constant in parallel = L/(x/2) = 2L/x = 2k.

written.text: A spring is stretched 20 mm by a load of 40 N. Calculate the value of spring constant. If an object causes an extension of 16 mm, what will be its weight?

rubric.why: The extension must be used consistently in SI units when calculating spring constant in N m⁻¹.
rubric.description: Convert the first extension to metres.

rubric.why: The spring constant follows from k = F/x.
rubric.how: Substitute k = 40/0.020 = 2000 N m⁻¹ = 2 kN m⁻¹.

rubric.why: The second extension must be converted consistently for F = kx.
The final force is the requested weight and must agree with the spring relationship.

modelAnswer: Extension x = 20 mm = 0.020 m.
Spring constant, k = F/x = 40/0.020 = 2000 N m⁻¹ = 2 kN m⁻¹.
For extension 16 mm, x = 0.016 m.

explain.title: Deforming force
explain.body: Your textbook defines a deforming force as an external force applied on an object that can change its size or shape. Stretching a spring increases its length; compression reduces it.

explain.title: Elasticity
explain.body: Your textbook defines an elastic object as: “An object is said to be elastic, if after removal of the deforming force, it restores to its original size and shape.” The property of the material is called elasticity.

explain.title: Inelastic materials and elastic limit
explain.body: Some materials, such as clay dough or plasticine, do not return to their original shape after the deforming force is removed; your textbook calls them inelastic materials. Beyond the elastic limit, the change becomes permanent and the material does not regain its original shape or size.

explain.title: Spring constant
explain.body: For a spring, spring constant is force divided by extension: k = F/x. Use force in newtons and extension in metres to obtain k in N m⁻¹. A larger k means more force is needed for the same extension.

mistakes: Calling any changed shape elastic without checking whether the object returns to its original size and shape when the force is removed.
Saying that an object remains elastic beyond its elastic limit; beyond that limit the change becomes permanent.
Using millimetres without converting to metres when calculating k in N m⁻¹.
Reversing the spring-constant formula: use k = F/x, not x/F.
Giving a Hooke's law statement without specifying the range in which force and extension are proportional.
